title: Kami Rita: 32 Everest Summits
excerpt: On 18 May 2026, Kami Rita Sherpa summited Everest for the 32nd time in his life, breaking his own record once again. Who is this man, and why are Sherpas the best climbers in the world?
seoTitle: Kami Rita Sherpa Summits Everest for the 32nd Time

content.value: On 18 May 2026, at 10:12 in the morning Nepal time, one man stood on the summit of Everest for the 32nd time in his life. Kami Rita Sherpa, 56, a professional guide from the village of Thame in the Solukhumbu district, broke his own world record again: more ascents to the highest point on Earth than any other person in history.
Who is Kami Rita Sherpa?

Kami Rita was born in 1970 in the village of Thame, in the Khumbu region at the foot of Everest. The same village produced Tenzing Norgay, who, alongside the New Zealander Sir Edmund Hillary, made the first ascent of Everest in history, on 29 May 1953.

Kami Rita's first ascent came in 1994, when he was 24. Since then, over three decades, he has returned to the summit almost every year. Only three years are missing from the list: 2014 (the Khumbu Icefall disaster that killed 16 Sherpas), 2015 (the devastating Nepal earthquake that closed the mountain) and 2020 (the global closure due to COVID-19). In some seasons he managed two summits.

Kami Rita is not a tourist on the mountain. He is not climbing for himself. Every one of his 32 ascents was made in a professional capacity: as a guide, an expedition leader, or responsible for fixing ropes or setting up high camps. His most recent ascent was made for his company.
In the same season, Lakpa Sherpa, 52, completed her 11th ascent of the summit, the undisputed women's world record.

content.value: Why Sherpas are the best climbers in the world

When you look at the Everest record books, the picture is clear: 11 of the 12 climbers who have summited Everest the most times in history are Sherpas. The first non-Sherpa on the list, the British guide Kenton Cool, has 19 ascents, 13 fewer than Kami Rita. Behind him are the Americans Dave Hahn and Garrett Madison, with 15 ascents each.

content.title: ✦ The numbers speak
content.value: 11 of the 12 climbers who have summited Everest the most times in history are Sherpas. Kami Rita, with 32 ascents, leads that list, 13 summits ahead of the first non-Sherpa on it.
The reason for this gap is a combination of genetics, culture and professional tradition.
The physiological side

Sherpas, born at altitude, carry distinct evolutionary adaptations to oxygen-thin environments. Research has identified EPAS1 gene variants in Sherpa populations that allow more efficient blood flow and higher metabolic efficiency under hypoxic conditions. They also tend to produce less excess hemoglobin, a condition that raises the risk of blood clots in high-altitude climbers whose bodies generate too many red blood cells.
The cultural side

In the Solukhumbu, mountaineering is not a hobby. It is a family profession passed from parents to children for three generations, since 1953. Children grow up knowing the routes, practicing glacier travel, and developing an intuitive feel for what a mountain does and when it becomes dangerous.
The practical side

Every climber who arrives at Everest today, whether an amateur from Europe, a professional climber from Asia or a veteran guide from America, depends on infrastructure the Sherpas built. The fixed ropes on the standard route? Sherpas set them. The ladders bridging the Khumbu Icefall crevasses? Sherpas placed them. The oxygen at the high camps? Sherpas carried it. Food, tents, heating: all Sherpas.

content.value: The 2026 Everest season: one of the most difficult in recent years
Kami Rita's record did not fall in a quiet season. 2026 was one of the most complicated Everest seasons in recent years, and still he summited.

At the end of April, a massive block of ice collapsed and blocked the Khumbu Icefall, the most dangerous section of the south side route and the bottleneck through which all climbers must pass. Hundreds of climbers were stranded at base camp for days, until the Icefall Doctors, the Sherpa team that maintains the route, managed to reset ladders and ropes and reopen it.

Nepal's Department of Tourism issued 492 climbing permits for Everest that season, a high number that reignited the debate about traffic jams near the summit. In the space of a month, three Nepali climbers died on Everest, a sharp reminder that even in the age of bottled oxygen, fixed ropes and precise weather forecasts, Everest remains a mountain that exacts a price.
At 56, Kami Rita showed no sign of stopping. Those who know him understand: when the expeditions return to Everest, the best bet is that he will be there again, perhaps with 33 behind him.

content.value: The way to Everest does not begin with gear, a budget or a government permit. It begins with a decision to go. For most people looking for an authentic Himalayan experience, the best way to get close to Everest is the Everest Base Camp trek, 12 to 14 days of walking that ends at the very place where Tenzing, Hillary and Kami Rita began their ascents.

content.value: Frequently asked questions
How many times has Kami Rita Sherpa summited Everest?
As of May 2026, Kami Rita has summited Everest 32 times, more than any other person in history. He has climbed it almost every year since his first ascent in 1994.
Where is Kami Rita Sherpa from?
From the village of Thame in the Khumbu region at the foot of Everest, the same village that produced Tenzing Norgay, who made the first ascent of Everest with Sir Edmund Hillary in 1953.
Why are Sherpas the best climbers in the world?

A combination of three factors: physiology, with genetic adaptations that allow more efficient blood circulation at altitude; culture, with mountaineering passed down as a family profession since 1953; and practical experience accumulated over decades of professional work on the highest routes in the world.
Does Kami Rita climb for personal pleasure?
No. Every one of his 32 ascents was made in a professional capacity: as a guide, expedition leader, rope fixer or high camp manager. He climbs to do his job and to lead others safely to the summit.
How can I experience Everest without climbing it?

Through the Everest Base Camp trek, 12 to 14 days of walking through the Khumbu that ends at the starting point of every major Everest expedition on the Nepal side. No technical climbing is required, and HighAir runs this trek every year.
